articles.description:
On-the-fly zstd blocks the NGINX event loop. ngx_mzstd on a thread pool against tokers/zstd-nginx-module: p99 latency, requests per second, CPU time and memory.
With tokers/zstd-nginx-module, zstd compression runs inside the NGINX worker’s event loop. While large responses were compressed at levels 3 and 19, the p99 latency of small uncompressed requests on the same worker rose from 1.9 ms to 4.2–198 ms, and to 1.5 s when 8 large requests arrived at once.
ngx_mzstd with zstd_thread_pool compresses on NGINX thread pools. In the same test, the p99 of small requests stayed at 1.7–2.0 ms, the same as with no compression.
One NGINX worker with a 4-thread pool served 2.2–15 times as many zstd responses per second as tokers/zstd-nginx-module on 85 KB–2.2 MB files, the most at levels 15 and 19.
Wi…
articles.title: zstd on NGINX thread pools: ngx_mzstd vs zstd-nginx-module

Code review is where a lot of shipping velocity silently goes to wait. The work is done and the PR is open, but it sits in a queue behind everyone else's changes while its author shifts to the next thing. When a reviewer eventually gets to it, they're often reading under time pressure, so the issues that slip through tend not to be the clear ones. They're the subtle logic and cross-file problems that surface later in production, long after the diff felt fine.
That gap between how much code teams ship and how carefully they can really review it is where AI code review tools now live. The question is no longer whether to use one. It's which one, and how much of the review you're prepared to trust it with.

articles.author: Srikar Phani Kumar Marti
articles.description:
You’ve been there: your Angular component’s UI stubbornly refuses to update even though you’re sure you changed the signal’s value. No errors, no crashes, just silence.
I had this happen recently while refactoring a component’s state to use Angular Signals. I was updating a signal that held an object, but the UI didn’t react. After some head-scratching, I realized the problem wasn’t Angular’s reactivity itself but the form of the signal, how the signal stored and exposed its value.
At first glance, a signal is just a container for a value you can get or set. But under the hood, Angular Signals can hold primitives, objects, arrays, or even computed values. How this data is shaped and updated determines if Angular’s change detection triggers.
To put it simply, the form of a signal is about w…
articles.title: Why Signal Forms Matter in Angular: The Subtle Traps and How to Avoid Them

articles.author: Akhouri Anmol Kumar
articles.description:
Description 👇
"Just use AES-256" is the most repeated and least useful sentence in security.
Ciphers almost never break. What breaks is everything around them: a guessable password, a reused nonce, ciphertext nobody authenticated, a key derived with the wrong function. This post is a tour of the whole stack: AES, ChaCha20, Argon2id, HKDF, HMAC, X25519, Ed25519 and Shamir's Secret Sharing. For each one: how it works, why it exists, when to pick it, and how the pieces fit together.
We'll also look at a real implementation as a worked example: ATLOCK v5, a pure-Python security suite from Akhouri Systems, packaged as a single .exe. Seeing these ideas as design decisions in shipping code beats textbook diagrams.
TL;DR
AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are both excellent. Pick by hardware and b…
articles.title: Encryption, Explained Properly: AES vs ChaCha20 vs Argon2id (and How to Actually Combine Them)

articles.author: The Block Research
articles.description:
Layer 2 scaling solutions help blockchains like Ethereum process more activity without forcing every transaction to happen directly on the base chain.
Ethereum’s main network is secure and decentralized, but blockspace is limited. When demand rises, fees increase and users can get priced out. Layer 2s address this by moving transaction activity to scaling systems that sit around Ethereum while still using it for settlement, security, data posting, or verification.
The most important Layer 2 designs today are rollups. Rollups process transactions off-chain, bundle them together, and post data or proofs back to Ethereum. This makes transactions cheaper and faster while keeping a connection to Ethereum’s trust foundation.
articles.title: Layer 2 Scaling Solutions
